name: Beijing
info: Beijing is the capital of China, in the north of the country. Known in turn as Ji, Youzhou, Nanjing, Zhongdu, Dadu and Beiping, it was a frontier city before becoming an imperial capital under the Jin, Yuan, Ming and Qing.

facts.founded: The city states of Ji and Yan were given to their rulers by King Wu of Zhou in the 11th century BCE according to Sima Qian; the Beijing Government uses 1045 BCE as the official estimate of the date
facts.where: On the northern edge of the North China Plain, with mountains on three sides, near the Yongding River, in northern China
facts.known: The Forbidden City; capital under the Jin, Yuan, Ming and Qing; Dadu of Kublai Khan; the Temple of Heaven; the Legation Quarter; the May Fourth Movement; Tiananmen Square; the Beijing dialect
facts.today: Beijing is the capital of the People's Republic of China and a provincial-level municipality with 16 districts.

t: Beijing began as the walled city of Ji, a frontier seat on the northern edge of China proper, and was a provincial town for about a thousand years.
It became a capital under the Jin in 1153, the Mongol Yuan from 1271 and the Ming from 1421, which gave it the plan and monuments it still has.
It was named Ji, Youzhou, Nanjing, Zhongdu, Dadu, Beiping and Beijing, and its name and standing changed again in 1928, 1937 and 1949.
dyk: Beijing, the Northern Capital, took its name in 1403 to distinguish it from Nanjing, the Southern Capital. It lost the name in 1928, regained it under Japanese occupation in 1937, lost it again in 1945 and recovered it in 1949.
ev: The Zhou confer the city states of Ji and Yan, the date being the Beijing Government's official estimate
The Liao rename Youzhou Nanjing and make it a secondary capital
The Jin move their capital to Yanjing and name it Zhongdu
Kublai Khan founds the Yuan dynasty and names his capital Dadu
The Yongle Emperor renames Beiping as Beijing
The Manchus take the city and make it the seat of the Qing dynasty
The Eight-Nation Alliance lifts the siege of the Legation Quarter and occupies the city
Mao Zedong proclaims the People's Republic of China from Tiananmen

sections.origins:
The earliest traces of habitation in the Beijing municipality are in the caves of Dragon Bone Hill near Zhoukoudian, where Peking Man, Homo erectus, lived; Homo sapiens used the caves from about 27,000 to 10,000 years ago. Over 40 Neolithic settlements and burial sites show that farming was widespread in the area 6,000 to 7,000 years ago.

The earliest events of the city's history are legend. According to Sima Qian, the Yellow Emperor defeated the Yan Emperor at Banquan in the 26th century BCE, possibly near Yanqing, and the sage-king Yao is said to have founded a town called Youdu in the region about 4,000 years ago. You, or Youzhou, later became one of the city's names.

The first event with archaeological support belongs to the 11th century BCE, when the Zhou dynasty absorbed the Shang. According to Sima Qian, King Wu of Zhou conferred titles on the rulers of the city states of Ji and Yan, and the Beijing Government uses 1045 BCE as the official estimate of the date. The seat of Ji, Jicheng, is believed to have stood in the south-west of present urban Beijing, near Guang'anmen, beside a steady supply of water from the Lotus Pool. Yan had its capital at Dongjialin, about 45 km to the south, where a large walled settlement and over 200 tombs have been found. Both lay on a trade route along the eastern flank of the Taihang Mountains. Some time in the Western Zhou or early Eastern Zhou, Yan conquered Ji and moved its capital there.
sections.growth:
For about a thousand years after the First Emperor, the city was a provincial seat on the northern edge of China proper. In the early Western Han the four counties of the Principality of Guangyang had 20,740 households and an estimated population of 70,685; in 57 CE the five counties of Guangyang Commandery had 44,550 households and an estimated 280,600 residents. In 742 the ten counties of Youzhou had 67,242 households and 371,312 residents.

The city's stature grew from the 10th century. Under the Liao, the population inside the walled city rose from 22,000 in 938 to 150,000 in 1113. After the Jin made it their Central Capital in 1153 and doubled its size, it grew from 82,000 in 1125 to 400,000 in 1207. Paper money was first issued in Beijing during the Jin, and the Lugou Bridge was built in 1189.

Dadu, begun in 1267, was nearly twice the size of Zhongdu. Its population was 418,000 in 1270 and 952,000 by 1327. Water came from the Jinshui and Gaoliang rivers and from channels built by the hydrologist Guo Shoujing, and the Tonghui Canal, completed in 1293, brought barges from Tongzhou to the lakes inside the city. The Ming built the Forbidden City and the Temple of Heaven between 1403 and 1420; the city had 960,000 residents in 1448, with 2.19 million in the surrounding region, and by the 15th century had essentially taken its current shape. Under the Qing it had 776,242 residents in 1781.
sections.rulers:
The state of Yan held Ji until the Qin took the city in 226 BCE; it became the seat of Guangyang Commandery, and under the Han the capital of the Kingdom of Yan and then of Youzhou. In 352 Murong Jun moved the capital of the Xianbei Former Yan from Manchuria to Ji, making it a sovereign capital for the first time in over 500 years; five years later it moved to Ye. The Sui renamed the area Zhuo Commandery, and under the Tang it was Youzhou again, with a military commander who held it largely autonomously for 150 years after the rebellion of An Lushan in 755.

In 936 the Later Jin ceded Youzhou to the Khitan Liao, who made it Nanjing, the Southern Capital, in 938. The Jurchen Jin took it in 1122 as Yanjing; the Song held it briefly in 1123 as Yanshan, and the Jin retook it in 1125. In 1153 Wanyan Liang moved the Jin capital there and named it Zhongdu. After the Mongols took the city in 1215, Kublai Khan had Dadu built, also known by the Mongol name Khanbaliq, and in 1279, when the last of the Song fell, it became for the first time the capital of the whole of China.

In 1368 the Ming took Dadu and renamed it Beiping. Zhu Di, Prince of Yan, took the throne in 1402 as the Yongle Emperor and in 1403 renamed it Beijing, the Northern Capital. It became the main capital in 1421, and the Qing made it their seat in 1644. The Republic kept the capital in Beijing until 1928, when the Nationalists moved it to Nanjing and the city became Beiping again. Under Japanese occupation from 1937 it was Beijing once more, and in 1949 it became the capital of the People's Republic.
sections.life:
The Liao kept the Tang plan of the city, with eight gates in the outer wall, an inner walled city converted into a palace complex, and 26 residential neighbourhoods. Khitan, Xi, Shiwei and Balhae people from the north and Han from the south settled in it. The Niujie Mosque dates from 996, the Fayuan Temple from 645 and the Tianning Temple from 1100 to 1119.

Dadu was laid out in a checkerboard of avenues 25 m wide and narrow lanes called hutongs, 6 to 7 m wide, with the main markets at Dongsi, Xisi and the north shore of Jishuitan. Builders came from across the Mongol empire, including Nepal and Central Asia: the White Stupa Temple of 1271 was designed by the Nepali architect Araniko. Marco Polo, Ibn Battuta, Odoric of Pordenone and Giovanni di Monte Corvino left accounts of visits, and the playwrights Ma Zhiyuan, Guan Hanqing and Wang Shifu lived there.

Under the Ming the Jesuit Matteo Ricci became an adviser to the Wanli Emperor in 1601 and founded the Nantang Cathedral in 1605. Residents, who had burned wood, turned to coal as the forests around the city disappeared. The Qing assigned the Eight Banners to live near the eight gates of the Inner City. In 1728 the Yongzheng Emperor ordered that candidates in the civil service examination speak Beijing Mandarin, and the Beijing dialect became the national standard for spoken Chinese in 1913. Peking Opera formed in the mid-19th century from Anhui and Hubei troupes invited to court. Tongrentang opened in 1669, and Quanjude, which introduced the hung oven, in 1864.
sections.crises:
In 979 the Song emperor Taizong besieged Nanjing and was defeated at the Battle of Gaoliang River. In 1214 Genghis Khan besieged Zhongdu and withdrew after a treaty; he besieged it again, and in 1215, after many inhabitants had starved, its defenders surrendered and it was looted and burned. In 1449 Esen Tayisi marched on the city with the captured Zhengtong Emperor, and was repelled. Epidemics in 1643 claimed 200,000 lives, and in March 1644 Li Zicheng's forces took the city and the Chongzhen Emperor hanged himself.

In 1860 Anglo-French forces took the city, and Lord Elgin ordered the Old Summer Palace burned in retaliation for the mistreatment of Western prisoners. In June 1900 Qing forces and Boxers besieged the Legation Quarter, which sheltered several hundred foreigners and about 3,200 Chinese Christians; the Eight-Nation Alliance lifted the siege, looted the city and occupied it. The Japanese occupation from 1937 spared the city urban fighting, but a Japanese biological warfare unit, North China Unit 1855, released cholera in southern Beijing in 1943, killing 1,872 residents.

In 1958 and 1959 about 420,000 residents were sent to the countryside during the shortages of the Great Leap Forward. In the Cultural Revolution Red Guards ransacked 114,000 homes in a month, and at least 1,772 residents were killed in August and September 1966. On 3 and 4 June 1989 troops fired on protesters in and around Tiananmen Square; hundreds of civilians were killed, thousands wounded and thousands detained, and the government has barred reporting or remembrance of the events.
sections.legacy:
Beijing has been China's capital for most of the time since 1279, and the Beijing dialect is its standard speech: the Republic adopted it in 1913, the Nationalists confirmed it in 1932 and the People's Republic in 1955. The Forbidden City, opened to the public as the Palace Museum after Puyi was evicted in 1924, the Temple of Heaven, the Summer Palace, the Ming Tombs and the Zhoukoudian Peking Man Site are among eight UNESCO World Heritage Sites in the city.

Peking University was founded in 1898. The American Indemnity College, set up in 1911 with Boxer indemnity funds as a preparatory school, became Tsinghua University in 1912. On 4 May 1919 about 3,000 students gathered in Tiananmen Square against the Treaty of Versailles, a protest that began a tradition of student activism in the city. On 1 October 1949 Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic from Tiananmen. Tiananmen Square was expanded and the Great Hall of the People and the National Museum were completed by 1959; the Ming city walls were pulled down in the 1960s for the subway and the 2nd Ring Road.

The city has since spread outward along ring roads, lost many old hutong neighbourhoods and hosted the 2008 Summer Olympics. It is the capital of the People's Republic of China, with a municipal population of about 22 million.

summary: Beijing began as the frontier city of Ji and grew into a capital under the Jin, Yuan, Ming and Qing, changing its name as its standing changed. It was the capital of the Republic until 1928 and has been the capital of the People's Republic of China since 1949.
references: Lillian Li, Beijing: From Imperial Capital to Olympic City (Palgrave Macmillan, 2007)
Madeleine Yue Dong, Republican Beijing: The City and Its Histories (University of California Press, 2003)
Gaohua Chen, The Capital of the Yuan Dynasty (Silkroad Press, 2015)
Jun Wang, Beijing Record: A Physical and Political History of Planning Modern Beijing (World Scientific, 2010)
David Strand, Rickshaw Beijing: City People and Politics in the 1920s (University of California Press, 1993)
notes: Disagreements: Peking Man's dates (History of Beijing: 770,000 to 230,000 years ago; Beijing: 230,000 to 250,000), so no dates given. Dadu's construction (History: began 1267, palace 1274, city by 1285, founded 1271; Beijing: 1264 to 1293). Genghis Khan's siege (History: 1214 siege, surrender and burning 1215; Beijing: besieged 1213, razed 1215). Boxer indemnity (History: 450 million taels at 4 percent; Beijing: US$335 million over 39 years), so no figure given. PLA entry (History: 3 February 1949; Beijing: 31 January 1949), left out. Beiping renamed in 1928 (Beijing: 28 June) left undated by day. Sui reunification (History 589; Beijing 581), left out. Forbidden City dating (History: reconstruction 1403 to 1420; Beijing: 1406 to 1420); I used 1403 to 1420 for the programme of building, which History says included the Forbidden City and Temple of Heaven. Ming move of capital: History 1421, Beijing 28 October 1420 (officially designated); I give 1421 in the rulers section and use 1420 only for the end of building. Largest city in the world: History says 1425 to 1635 and 1710 to 1825, Beijing says generally believed most of the 15th to 18th centuries, so left out; the sections give only the 1448 and 1781 figures.

Left out on purpose: the 'Four Pests' campaign, most of the 1976 to 1989 and later events (Democracy Wall, Olympics detail, SARS, pollution, economy, rankings), as tourism or rankings or not needed. 1989 is told in one sentence with the article's wording (hundreds killed, thousands wounded and detained); the article gives no total figure and says the government bars research. The Cultural Revolution figures (114,000 homes, at least 1,772 killed) are from History of Beijing; Beijing gives 4,922 of 6,843 designated sites destroyed or damaged, which I left out for space.

Doubts: start -1045 is the Beijing Government's official estimate for the Zhou conferral, not a founding of the city as such (circa true); the 'Today' fact uses 'provincial-level municipality with 16 districts' from the city article. The first-paragraph dates for the Western Han counts (no year given for the 70,685 figure beyond 'early Western Han'). Hedge in legacy 'for most of the time since 1279' follows History's own list (interludes 1368 to 1420 and 1928 to 1949).

Wanted but not found: when the name Ji gave way to Youzhou for the city (History says gradually; Tang era). No population figure for the Qing after 1881-82 other than 776,111 (not used). Nothing on the Liao name Yanjing's meaning beyond 'Yan Capital' use.
